--- title: Nonparametric Smooths with HSGP author: - name: PyMC Labs description: Fit a flexible 1-D nonparametric smooth with the hsgp() term — a Hilbert Space Gaussian Process approximation — and intervene on it with do(). tags: - Gaussian Process - HSGP - Nonparametric image: thumbnails/hsgp_1d.png jupyter: pathmc bibliography: "../../../docs/references.bib" bread-crumbs: false --- Most pathmc terms are linear in their coefficients. Sometimes the relationship between a predictor and an outcome is smooth but *not* linear — a dose–response curve, a trend over a continuous index, a smooth confounder adjustment. The `hsgp()` term adds such a smooth via a **Hilbert Space Gaussian Process** approximation [@riutort2023practical], the same scalable construction exposed by [Bambi's `hsgp()`](https://bambinos.github.io/bambi/notebooks/hsgp_1d.html). An HSGP approximates a Gaussian process with a finite basis of Laplacian eigenfunctions, so it reduces to a linear model in a fixed basis matrix. That makes it fast, differentiable, and — because the basis is a deterministic function of the input `pm.Data` — fully compatible with `do()` interventions. ## Simulated data We draw a smooth signal and add observation noise. The input is deliberately *not* centered on zero to exercise the internal centering of the basis. ::: {#bbfdcf5b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import pathmc rng = np.random.default_rng(0) x = np.linspace(10.0, 20.0, 120) true = np.sin((x - 10.0) * 0.9) y = true + rng.normal(0.0, 0.2, size=x.size) df = pd.DataFrame({"x": x, "y": y}) ``` ::: ## The model `hsgp(x, m=..., c=...)` is a standalone term: `m` sets the number of basis vectors and `c` the boundary-expansion factor. The smooth carries its own basis weights, so it takes no coefficient prefix. ::: {#5bcbcebd .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} model = pathmc.model("y ~ hsgp(x, m=20, c=1.5)", data=df) model.equations() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=2} $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{y} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ ell_{y_x} &\sim \text{InverseGamma}(alpha=3,\, beta=1) \\ \eta_{y_x} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \beta_{hsgp_y_x} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=1) \\[6pt] \mu_{y} &= \beta_{0,\,y} + f_{\mathrm{hsgp}}(\mathrm{x}) \\ \mathrm{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{y},\, \sigma_{y}) \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: The default priors expose the kernel amplitude (`eta_y_x`), lengthscale (`ell_y_x`), and standardized basis weights (`beta_hsgp_y_x`): ::: {#dcc80354 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} model.priors() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=3} $$ \begin{aligned} \beta_{y} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\ \sigma_{y} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ ell_{y_x} &\sim \text{InverseGamma}(alpha=3,\, beta=1) \\ \eta_{y_x} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\ \beta_{hsgp_y_x} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=1) \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: ## Fit and recover the smooth ::: {#a0686ff9 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} idata = model.fit(random_seed=0) f_mean = idata.posterior["f_y_x"].mean(("chain", "draw")).values np.corrcoef(f_mean - f_mean.mean(), true - true.mean())[0, 1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` NUTS[nutpie]: [eta_y_x, ell_y_x, beta_hsgp_y_x, beta_y, sigma_y] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} 

```

The posterior-mean smooth tracks the true function closely. To show that honestly we plot the posterior of `mu_y` — the full linear predictor, which already carries the intercept — as a mean line with a 94% highest-density interval, rather than recentering `f_y_x` by hand.

::: {#cell-fig-hsgp-recovery .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"}
import arviz as az
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

mu = idata.posterior["mu_y"]
mu_mean = mu.mean(("chain", "draw")).values
hdi = az.hdi(mu, prob=0.94).values

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.scatter(x, y, s=12, alpha=0.5, color="C0", label="observed")
ax.fill_between(x, hdi[:, 0], hdi[:, 1], color="C1", alpha=0.3, label="94% HDI")
ax.plot(x, mu_mean, "C1", lw=2, label="posterior mean")
ax.plot(x, true, "k--", lw=1.5, label="true smooth")
ax.set(xlabel="x", ylabel="y")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Posterior mean of mu_y with its 94% HDI, against the true smooth. The band covers the true curve across the fitted range of x, and widens at the boundaries where the basis is least constrained by data.](hsgp_1d_files/figure-html/fig-hsgp-recovery-output-1.png){#fig-hsgp-recovery width=674 height=356}

## Intervening on the smooth

Because the basis recomputes from the input data node, `do()` propagates through the smooth. Interventions should stay within the fitted support of `x`: when `c` is used the boundary is derived from the fitted data, so a grid wider than the training range would extrapolate beyond the basis.

::: {#95478d72 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
low = model.do(set={"x": 12.0}).mean("y")
high = model.do(set={"x": 18.0}).mean("y")
low, high
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6}
```
(0.9411555417093392, 0.776024736422839)
```

## Scope

Phase 1 supports a single 1-D **exogenous** input on cross-sectional models. Multi-dimensional inputs, grouped (`by=`) GPs, and panel/scan models raise a clear error and are tracked as follow-ups.

The input must be exogenous because the basis is built by evaluating it: PyMC derives the centering midpoint and the boundary from the input's realized values. Smoothing an endogenous variable (one that is itself the outcome of another equation) would freeze the basis at a random prior draw, so `pathmc` rejects it rather than fitting a model whose result depends on compilation-time RNG.
